subtopic_detail: Panic attack presenting to ED - workup and immediate management
stem:
A 28-year-old woman self-presents to a metropolitan emergency department at 2200 hours with a 40-minute history of chest tightness, palpitations, breathlessness and a sense that she is about to die. This is her fourth similar attack in six weeks. Each attack has begun suddenly, peaked within about 10 minutes and settled within an hour. Between attacks she has become preoccupied with when the next one will occur and now avoids the local shopping centre where the second attack happened.

She has no personal history of asthma, cardiac disease or thyroid disease, takes only the combined oral contraceptive pill, drinks 2 standard drinks per week and does not use illicit substances. Her mother died suddenly at 61 of a myocardial infarction last year. On arrival she is anxious and tearful; on your review 30 minutes later she is settled and her symptoms have almost fully resolved.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92, BP 128/78, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7.
data_table.Examination: Chest clear, heart sounds dual with no added sounds, calves soft, no focal neurology.
data_table.Investigations: 12-lead ECG sinus rhythm rate 90 with no ischaemic changes, high-sensitivity troponin at 0 hours below the assay limit, venous blood gas with normal pH and lactate, TSH within reference from her GP two weeks ago.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her ED management?

options.text: Explain that her symptoms are consistent with a panic attack, discharge with written information and refer for a Mental Health Treatment Plan and CBT within one to two weeks
options.rationale: The episode pattern (recurrent, discrete, peak within 10 minutes, autonomic and cognitive symptoms with anticipatory worry and situational avoidance) meets DSM-5 panic disorder, and workup has excluded acute cardiac, respiratory, metabolic and endocrine causes. Psychoeducation plus timely CBT referral for interoceptive and situational exposure is first-line and reduces ED re-presentation (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Anxiety disorders; RANZCP CPG: Anxiety Disorders).

options.text: Repeat high-sensitivity troponin at 3 hours and arrange inpatient stress echocardiogram before any consideration of discharge from ED
options.rationale: Rule-out pathway for possible acute coronary syndrome requires a second troponin or a HEART/EDACS pathway decision, but in this low-risk woman with a clear behavioural pattern of discrete peak-fear episodes and negative first-line workup, cardiac admission is disproportionate and reinforces catastrophic health beliefs that maintain panic disorder (Source: NHF/CSANZ ACS Guidelines).

options.text: Prescribe diazepam 5 mg orally three times daily for two weeks as a scheduled course and arrange routine GP follow-up review within a fortnight
options.rationale: A scheduled benzodiazepine course reinforces the belief that panic is a physiological emergency requiring rescue medication, promotes rebound anxiety between doses and risks dependence; benzodiazepines are not first-line for panic disorder in AU guidance (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Anxiety disorders).

options.text: Commence propranolol 40 mg orally twice daily and arrange a 24-hour Holter monitor as an outpatient before any mental health referral is made
options.rationale: Propranolol has an evidence base only for time-limited performance-only social anxiety; it is not first-line for panic disorder, and Holter monitoring is not indicated in the absence of documented arrhythmia or syncope (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Admit for overnight cardiology observation and outpatient exercise stress test in the coming week before any mental health follow-up
options.rationale: Admission of a low-risk woman with a resolving anxiety attack and negative first-line workup reinforces illness beliefs, uses inpatient resources inappropriately, and delays the first-line psychological intervention (Source: RANZCP CPG: Anxiety Disorders).

explanation.summary: Recurrent discrete panic attacks with anticipatory worry and situational avoidance in a low-risk patient with a negative first-line cardiac and metabolic workup should be diagnosed as panic disorder in the ED. First-line management is psychoeducation and CBT referral, not benzodiazepines or cardiac admission.
key_points: DSM-5 panic disorder: recurrent unexpected attacks plus 1 month of worry or maladaptive change
First-line management is CBT with interoceptive exposure; SSRI is added if impairment persists
Benzodiazepines are avoided or used only briefly to bridge SSRI onset
Excessive investigation reinforces catastrophic health beliefs that maintain the disorder
explanation.pearls: In context, name the diagnosis explicitly to the patient. Naming panic disorder reduces catastrophic misinterpretation and is itself therapeutic.

subtopic_detail: Generalised social anxiety pharmacotherapy - SSRI vs propranolol discriminator
stem:
A 24-year-old graduate lawyer attends her GP after her firm rotated her onto a client-facing team. She reports that since university she has avoided any situation involving being observed by others: eating in the tearoom, speaking up in meetings, using public toilets and making phone calls. She feels intense fear of humiliation and has always managed by declining or delegating. Since the rotation four weeks ago she has had daily anticipatory nausea and has taken 12 sick days, and her partner has noticed she now avoids their local supermarket.

She drinks no alcohol, uses no substances, and has no cardiac or respiratory history. Her mother has treated social anxiety. She has never trialled psychological therapy or medication. She asks about propranolol because a friend takes it before job interviews and finds it works well.

data_table.Examination: Anxious, reduced eye contact, no depressive or psychotic features, insight preserved.
data_table.Investigations: TSH within reference from screening three months ago.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacological recommendation?

options.text: Propranolol 20 mg orally 30 minutes before any anticipated stressful social situation, taken as needed up to three times daily
options.rationale: Beta-blocker as-needed is supported only for isolated performance-type social anxiety (e.g. musical performance) and has no efficacy for the generalised, pervasive avoidance seen here; overuse would replace situational avoidance with pill-avoidance (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Social anxiety disorder).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Social anxiety disorder

options.text: Diazepam 2 mg orally daily as a short-term measure until formal psychological therapy is available in three months
options.rationale: Daily benzodiazepine for months creates tolerance and dependence, blunts exposure-based learning during CBT, and is not first-line for any anxiety disorder in AU guidance (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Anxiety disorders).

options.text: Moclobemide 300 mg orally twice daily as the recommended first-line pharmacotherapy for social anxiety disorder in Australia
options.rationale: Moclobemide has evidence in social anxiety but is second-line in AU guidance after SSRI or venlafaxine; MAOI-related dietary and interaction cautions make it a step-up choice (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Social anxiety disorder).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Social anxiety disorder

options.text: Escitalopram 10 mg orally daily alongside referral for CBT with graded in-vivo exposure to feared social situations
options.rationale: Generalised social anxiety disorder (pervasive across multiple situations, chronic since adolescence, marked functional impairment) is treated with an SSRI plus CBT; escitalopram or sertraline are first-line SSRIs with Level I evidence in the generalised subtype, and combination outperforms either modality alone at 12 months (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Social anxiety disorder; RANZCP CPG: Anxiety Disorders).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Social anxiety disorder

options.text: Mirtazapine 15 mg orally at night with GP review at four weeks and no formal psychology referral in the interim
options.rationale: Mirtazapine is not a first-line agent for social anxiety disorder; sedation and weight gain add burden without efficacy advantage, and CBT referral is the standard partner intervention (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: Generalised social anxiety disorder is treated first-line with an SSRI (escitalopram, sertraline, or paroxetine) plus CBT with graded exposure. Propranolol is reserved for isolated performance anxiety; benzodiazepines are avoided for maintenance treatment.
key_points: Generalised subtype = multiple domains of social fear with pervasive avoidance
Performance-only subtype = discrete situations (public speaking, music performance)
SSRI plus CBT beats either alone at 12 months
Propranolol works only for time-limited performance situations
explanation.pearls: In context, subtype the social anxiety before prescribing. The generalised versus performance-only distinction changes the drug class.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Social anxiety disorder

subtopic_detail: OCD - clomipramine trial after failed SSRI trials
stem:
A 36-year-old man with an 11-year history of contamination-themed OCD returns to your community mental health clinic. He has completed 20 sessions of exposure and response prevention with a psychologist over 18 months with partial response. His symptoms remain moderate with a Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale (Y-BOCS) score of 22 despite two adequate SSRI trials: fluoxetine at 80 mg orally daily for 14 weeks and sertraline at 200 mg orally daily for 12 weeks, each escalated in accordance with Australian OCD dosing.

He has no history of bipolar disorder, no cardiac disease, no epilepsy and no urinary retention. His most recent 12-lead ECG shows a QTc of 415 ms in sinus rhythm. He is otherwise well and highly motivated to keep trying pharmacotherapy before augmentation. He asks whether a different class of medication is worth attempting.

data_table.Examination: MSE unremarkable other than resistance to contamination obsessions and hand-washing rituals.
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, LFTs, TSH within reference from last month. 12-lead ECG sinus rhythm with QTc 415 ms.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological step?

options.text: Add risperidone 1 mg orally at night as the first augmentation step before trialling any further serotonergic monotherapy
options.rationale: Low-dose antipsychotic augmentation is a valid strategy but is generally attempted after a third serotonergic trial has failed, particularly when a distinct class such as clomipramine has never been tried; it also adds metabolic and extrapyramidal risk without addressing the underlying serotonergic mechanism (Source: RANZCP CPG: OCD).

options.text: Swap to venlafaxine XR 225 mg orally daily as the preferred evidence-based next serotonergic monotherapy for OCD in Australia
options.rationale: Venlafaxine has weaker OCD evidence than clomipramine and is not preferred as the third serotonergic monotherapy in AU guidance; it may be considered but is not the highest-yield next step (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - OCD).

options.text: Commence clomipramine 25 mg orally at night and titrate towards 150 to 250 mg daily with periodic ECG review of QTc
options.rationale: Clomipramine is the next-line monotherapy after failure of two adequate SSRI trials in OCD; it is the only tricyclic with proven OCD-specific efficacy through potent serotonin reuptake inhibition. Titration to 150 to 250 mg daily with baseline and follow-up ECG (target QTc under 500 ms) is standard, and his QTc of 415 ms is well within acceptable range to start (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - OCD; Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Combine sertraline 200 mg orally daily with fluoxetine 40 mg orally daily to increase overall serotonergic effect at receptor level
options.rationale: Combining two SSRIs adds serotonin toxicity risk without evidence of benefit and is not recommended; the alternative when one SSRI fails is switch to another SSRI or clomipramine, not combination (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Refer for deep brain stimulation of the ventral capsule as the appropriate next pharmacological step for his refractory OCD
options.rationale: Deep brain stimulation is reserved for severe treatment-refractory OCD after multiple pharmacological and psychological trials including clomipramine and augmentation, and is not the next pharmacological step (Source: RANZCP CPG: OCD).

explanation.summary: After two failed adequate SSRI trials in OCD, clomipramine is the highest-yield next monotherapy. Antipsychotic augmentation follows once serotonergic monotherapies are exhausted.
key_points: Adequate OCD SSRI trial: 12 weeks at maximal tolerated dose
Clomipramine target 150 to 250 mg daily; ECG monitoring for QTc
Augmentation with low-dose SGA is after clomipramine, not before
DBS is reserved for severe refractory OCD after failure of multiple pharmacological strategies
explanation.pearls: In context, the OCD treatment algorithm rewards persistence with high-dose serotonergic agents before switching mechanism. Y-BOCS anchors your assessment of trial success.

subtopic_detail: OCD SSRI target dose distinct from depression target dose
stem:
A 19-year-old university student is diagnosed with OCD after 12 months of contamination obsessions and 3 to 4 hours of daily hand-washing and shower rituals. Her Y-BOCS score is 24 and she is functionally impaired. She has been referred for ERP and you agree with the psychiatry registrar to commence fluvoxamine at the same time.

She has no cardiac, hepatic or renal disease. She takes no other medications and has no allergies. She asks how long it will take to know if the medication is working and what dose she should expect to reach.

data_table.Examination: Chapped hands with dermatitis; MSE otherwise unremarkable.
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, LFTs, TSH within reference.

lead_in: Which dose target and trial duration best matches the recommended OCD-specific regimen?

options.text: Fluvoxamine 100 mg orally daily reviewed at 4 weeks with switch to a different SSRI if no meaningful response is seen
options.rationale: 100 mg is a starting dose for depression and an inadequate dose target for OCD; reviewing at 4 weeks would prompt premature switching (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Fluvoxamine 50 mg orally daily indefinitely with no planned dose titration or scheduled treatment review appointment
options.rationale: 50 mg daily is the initiation dose only; without titration this is a subtherapeutic OCD trial (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Fluvoxamine 400 mg orally daily reviewed at 6 weeks as a maximum-effect strategy given her marked functional impairment
options.rationale: 400 mg exceeds the AMH maximum daily dose for fluvoxamine (300 mg), and 6 weeks is too short to declare an OCD trial failed (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Fluvoxamine 100 mg orally daily plus lorazepam 1 mg orally three times daily to accelerate anxiolytic response early on
options.rationale: The dose is subtherapeutic for OCD and lorazepam adds no efficacy while creating dependence risk and interfering with ERP; benzodiazepines have no primary role in OCD (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Anxiety disorders).

options.text: Fluvoxamine 200 to 300 mg orally daily reviewed at a minimum of 10 to 12 weeks after target dose is reached
options.rationale: OCD requires higher SSRI doses than depression and a longer trial before response is assessed; fluvoxamine target is 200 to 300 mg daily for at least 10 to 12 weeks before declaring the trial failed. This dose-and-duration pattern applies across the SSRI class in OCD (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - OCD; Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: OCD requires SSRI doses at the top of the licensed range and a trial of at least 10 to 12 weeks before declaring failure. Applying depression dosing timelines produces premature diagnosis of treatment resistance.
key_points: OCD SSRI targets are 2 to 3 times depression targets
Fluvoxamine 200 to 300 mg, fluoxetine 40 to 80 mg, sertraline 150 to 200 mg, escitalopram 20 mg, paroxetine 40 to 60 mg
Minimum trial 10 to 12 weeks at target dose before switch
First-line therapy is ERP alone or ERP plus SSRI depending on severity
explanation.pearls: In context, warn patients that OCD response is slow and partial. Setting the timeline at the first consult prevents premature abandonment of an adequate trial.

stem:
A 41-year-old paramedic presents to his GP nine months after a mass-casualty road traffic incident. He describes vivid intrusive memories of the scene, nightly nightmares, hypervigilance while driving, avoidance of the section of highway involved and marked emotional numbing towards his wife and children. His alcohol use has doubled to 6 standard drinks per night as a way of getting to sleep. He has taken 14 sick days in the last three months.

He asks specifically for diazepam because a colleague has been given it and reports feeling better on it. He has no history of substance dependence prior to this year, no bipolar disorder and no psychotic symptoms. He accepts referral for trauma-focused therapy but says he needs something for the meantime.

data_table.Examination: Anxious, avoidant eye contact, hypervigilant to background noise; no thought disorder or psychosis.
data_table.Investigations: PCL-5 score 58. AUDIT-C 8. LFTs mildly raised (GGT 78 U/L, RR under 60). TSH within reference.

lead_in: Which is the best justification for declining his request for diazepam?

options.text: Benzodiazepines interact directly with SSRIs to cause serotonin syndrome and therefore cannot be safely co-prescribed in his case
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines do not act on the serotonin system and do not cause serotonin syndrome; the concern is misplaced (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Diazepam causes rebound flashbacks on cessation and is teratogenic in any male-partner co-prescription in the household
options.rationale: Teratogenicity is not relevant in this male patient and rebound flashbacks are not a recognised discontinuation phenomenon; the correct reason relates to extinction learning and dependence (Source: Phoenix Australia Australian Guidelines for PTSD).
source_refs: Phoenix Australia Australian Guidelines for PTSD

options.text: Diazepam is contraindicated in men over 40 years of age due to a well-documented falls risk and cognitive impairment profile
options.rationale: Age 40 is not a contraindication; falls risk is a real but general benzodiazepine consideration, not the PTSD-specific reason for avoiding them (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Benzodiazepines impair extinction learning central to trauma-focused therapy and add dependence risk on his escalating alcohol use
options.rationale: The Australian Phoenix Australia PTSD guidelines and international guidance recommend against benzodiazepines in PTSD: they impair fear-extinction learning central to trauma-focused CBT and EMDR, are associated with worse PTSD outcomes in longitudinal data, and pose particular dependence risk when combined with pre-existing alcohol misuse (Source: Phoenix Australia Australian Guidelines for PTSD; RANZCP CPG: PTSD).
source_refs: Phoenix Australia Australian Guidelines for PTSD

options.text: Benzodiazepines are only unhelpful here because of PBS restrictions on their long-term supply for anxiety indications in general practice
options.rationale: PBS restrictions on quantity are a system-level issue, not the clinical reason. The therapeutic reason is that benzodiazepines block extinction learning and worsen PTSD trajectory (Source: Phoenix Australia Australian Guidelines for PTSD).
source_refs: Phoenix Australia Australian Guidelines for PTSD

explanation.summary: The Phoenix Australia PTSD guidelines recommend against benzodiazepines in PTSD. Mechanistically they impair the fear-extinction learning that underpins trauma-focused therapy, and they carry particular risk when combined with alcohol misuse.
key_points: First-line PTSD psychotherapy: trauma-focused CBT or EMDR
First-line PTSD pharmacotherapy: sertraline or paroxetine
Benzodiazepines associated with worse PTSD outcomes and interfere with extinction learning
Prazosin is an option for treatment-resistant nightmares
explanation.pearls: In context, the request for a benzodiazepine is itself clinical data. Use it to open the trauma-focused therapy conversation rather than to prescribe.

sources.label: Phoenix Australia Australian Guidelines for PTSD

subtopic_detail: PTSD SSRI selection - sertraline vs paroxetine
stem:
A 29-year-old woman meets DSM-5 criteria for PTSD 8 months after a serious sexual assault. She has completed initial psychoeducation with her GP and is on a 6-month waiting list for a trauma-focused CBT program at her local community mental health service. She and her GP agree to commence an SSRI while she waits.

She hopes to conceive within the next 12 months and has stopped hormonal contraception. She has no cardiac, hepatic or renal disease and no drug allergies. She takes no other regular medication and asks which SSRI is the best first choice given her plans.

data_table.Examination: Intrusive memories, hyperarousal, avoidance and negative cognitions consistent with PTSD.
data_table.Investigations: TSH, FBC, UEC, LFTs within reference.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate first-line SSRI?

options.text: Fluoxetine 20 mg orally daily titrated to 60 mg as the preferred agent for PTSD in reproductive-age women
options.rationale: Fluoxetine has evidence in PTSD but is not TGA-registered for the indication and has a long half-life (norfluoxetine 7 to 15 days) that complicates any planned switch or discontinuation before conception (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Paroxetine 20 mg orally daily titrated to 40 mg as the preferred agent given TGA registration for PTSD in Australia
options.rationale: Paroxetine is one of two TGA-registered PTSD SSRIs but is pregnancy category D (association with cardiac malformations, particularly right ventricular outflow tract lesions); it is not preferred in a woman planning conception (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook; TGA Prescribing Medicines in Pregnancy).

options.text: Sertraline 50 mg orally daily titrated to a target of 100 to 200 mg over four to six weeks with regular review
options.rationale: Sertraline is TGA-registered for PTSD, is one of the two most evidence-based agents alongside paroxetine, and is the preferred SSRI in women of reproductive age who are planning pregnancy or breastfeeding due to favourable pregnancy and lactation data. Target 100 to 200 mg (Source: Phoenix Australia Australian Guidelines for PTSD; Australian Medicines Handbook).
source_refs: Phoenix Australia Australian Guidelines for PTSD

options.text: Mirtazapine 30 mg orally at night as an evidence-based first-line PTSD monotherapy in Australian primary care
options.rationale: Mirtazapine is a possible adjunct for PTSD-associated insomnia but is not first-line pharmacotherapy for the disorder (Source: Phoenix Australia Australian Guidelines for PTSD).
source_refs: Phoenix Australia Australian Guidelines for PTSD

options.text: Diazepam 5 mg orally three times daily as a short-term measure until trauma-focused therapy commences at 6 months
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines are recommended against in PTSD; they impair extinction learning and worsen longitudinal outcomes (Source: Phoenix Australia Australian Guidelines for PTSD).
source_refs: Phoenix Australia Australian Guidelines for PTSD

explanation.summary: Sertraline and paroxetine are the two SSRIs with the strongest PTSD evidence and are TGA-registered for the indication. Sertraline is preferred in women planning pregnancy because of superior pregnancy and lactation safety data.
key_points: First-line psychological therapy: trauma-focused CBT or EMDR
First-line SSRI: sertraline or paroxetine
Sertraline preferred in reproductive-age women planning pregnancy
Paroxetine pregnancy category D - cardiac malformation signal
explanation.pearls: In context, pregnancy planning changes the SSRI selection long before the patient conceives. Ask about pregnancy plans at every first prescription.

sources.label: Phoenix Australia Australian Guidelines for PTSD

subtopic_detail: EMDR vs trauma-focused CBT - patient-factor discriminator
stem:
A 34-year-old refugee man from Iran meets DSM-5 criteria for PTSD following torture in detention two years ago. He is fluent in Farsi but has limited English and speaks with the aid of a Farsi interpreter through your community clinic. He has no comorbid substance use disorder, no active psychosis and no acute suicidality. He finds writing distressing and disclosed that in his cultural context talking at length about the trauma feels shameful.

He is willing to engage with a psychological therapy but has previously stopped a group program that involved writing an account of his trauma. His psychologist offers a choice between trauma-focused CBT with imaginal exposure and written narrative, and eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing (EMDR).

data_table.Examination: MSE unremarkable other than PTSD features.

lead_in: Which factor most supports EMDR as the preferred first-line psychological therapy for this patient?

options.text: EMDR requires less verbal disclosure and no written narrative, aligning with his cultural context and prior drop-out from a written program
options.rationale: Both therapies are first-line for PTSD in AU guidance; the treatment-selection discriminator here is the modality fit. EMDR uses bilateral stimulation with brief target-image recall and requires less verbal narrative and no written trauma account than TF-CBT, aligning with his prior tolerance and cultural context (Source: Phoenix Australia Australian Guidelines for PTSD; RANZCP CPG: PTSD).
source_refs: Phoenix Australia Australian Guidelines for PTSD

options.text: EMDR is more effective than trauma-focused CBT for all adult PTSD patients according to current Australian guideline recommendations
options.rationale: Phoenix Australia guidelines rate EMDR and trauma-focused CBT as first-line with broadly comparable efficacy; superiority is not claimed and the choice is patient-preference and modality-fit driven (Source: Phoenix Australia Australian Guidelines for PTSD).
source_refs: Phoenix Australia Australian Guidelines for PTSD

options.text: EMDR is the only trauma-focused therapy that does not require an interpreter in his refugee context and Farsi language pairing
options.rationale: EMDR still requires an interpreter for accurate history-taking, safety planning and processing check-ins; the interpreter burden is comparable (Source: Phoenix Australia Australian Guidelines for PTSD).
source_refs: Phoenix Australia Australian Guidelines for PTSD

options.text: Trauma-focused CBT is explicitly contraindicated in all survivors of torture in the Australian refugee mental health model of care
options.rationale: TF-CBT is not contraindicated in survivors of torture; the Foundation House model routinely uses it. The issue for this patient is prior intolerance of a specific written-narrative program (Source: Foundation House (Vic) refugee mental health model of care).
source_refs: Foundation House (Vic) refugee mental health model of care

options.text: EMDR does not require any verbal or non-verbal recall of the trauma during any phase of the treatment protocol
options.rationale: EMDR requires brief non-verbal or verbal target-image recall during bilateral stimulation phases; it reduces but does not eliminate trauma engagement (Source: Phoenix Australia Australian Guidelines for PTSD).
source_refs: Phoenix Australia Australian Guidelines for PTSD

explanation.summary: Phoenix Australia lists both trauma-focused CBT and EMDR as first-line for PTSD. Treatment selection is driven by modality fit, cultural context, previous therapy history and patient preference, not claimed superiority of one over the other.
key_points: First-line psychological therapies for PTSD: TF-CBT and EMDR
TF-CBT typically involves detailed verbal or written trauma narrative
EMDR involves brief target-image recall with bilateral stimulation, less narrative-heavy
Choose based on patient preference and previous therapy tolerance
explanation.pearls: In context, refugee mental health should route through Foundation House (Vic) or STARTTS (NSW) where possible, as they run structured trauma-focused programs with trained interpreters.

sources.label: Phoenix Australia Australian Guidelines for PTSD
Foundation House (Vic) refugee mental health model of care

subtopic_detail: Adjustment disorder vs PTSD - Criterion A stressor threshold
stem:
A 46-year-old accountant presents to his GP three months after being made redundant from a role he had held for 18 years. He describes persistent low mood, tearfulness, poor sleep with early morning waking and reduced appetite. He ruminates about lost identity and worries constantly about the family mortgage. He denies intrusive re-experiencing, flashbacks, nightmares or hypervigilance. He has not avoided any specific reminders of work; he still meets colleagues socially and drives past his old office without distress.

He has no personal or family history of mood disorder. He drinks 4 standard drinks weekly, does not use other substances and has no active suicidal ideation. His symptoms have caused him to withdraw from his weekly football team and he has been unable to update his CV or apply for new roles.

data_table.Examination: Tearful, low mood, no psychomotor retardation, no psychotic features. K-10 score 26.

lead_in: Which is the single most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Persistent complex bereavement disorder secondary to identity loss
options.rationale: This DSM-5-TR condition applies to prolonged grief after death of a close attachment; redundancy is not bereavement in the diagnostic sense (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Post-traumatic stress disorder secondary to job loss
options.rationale: PTSD requires exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury or sexual violence (DSM-5 Criterion A). Redundancy, though highly distressing, does not meet this threshold and there are no intrusion, avoidance, cognition or arousal symptoms characteristic of PTSD (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Adjustment disorder with mixed anxiety and depressed mood
options.rationale: Adjustment disorder describes emotional or behavioural symptoms in response to an identifiable stressor (redundancy) beginning within 3 months, out of proportion to the stressor and causing functional impairment, that do not meet criteria for another disorder. Absence of PTSD Criterion A trauma and absence of full major depressive episode criteria place him here (Source: DSM-5-TR; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Major depressive disorder single episode, moderate severity
options.rationale: MDD requires 5 or more of the 9 SIGECAPS symptoms for at least 2 weeks with depressed mood or anhedonia; this vignette describes fewer clearly present neurovegetative and cognitive symptoms and the mood is reactive to circumstance, favouring adjustment disorder (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Generalised anxiety disorder with depressive features
options.rationale: GAD requires excessive worry across multiple domains on more days than not for 6 months or more; his worry is 3 months in duration, tied to one dominant stressor, and does not meet the multi-domain chronic pattern (Source: DSM-5-TR).

explanation.summary: PTSD is gated by the Criterion A stressor: actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violence. Redundancy, divorce, financial loss and similar life events, even when highly distressing, are non-Criterion-A stressors and produce adjustment disorder when they impair function.
key_points: PTSD Criterion A stressor: death/serious injury/sexual violence, direct/witnessed/close-relative/first-responder-repeated
Adjustment disorder: response to identifiable stressor within 3 months, subthreshold for MDD/GAD/PTSD
Duration: acute under 6 months, persistent 6 months or more
First-line management: psychological support, problem-solving therapy, address stressor
explanation.pearls: In context, adjustment disorder is common and under-diagnosed. Do not upgrade to PTSD in the absence of Criterion A - the treatment pathway differs and misdiagnosis creates unnecessary trauma-focused therapy referrals.

subtopic_detail: Complex PTSD (ICD-11) - disturbances in self-organisation triad
stem:
A 33-year-old woman presents to a community mental health clinic with a history of chronic sexual and physical abuse by a family member between ages 6 and 15. She describes persistent intrusive memories, nightmares, avoidance of anything connected to the perpetrator and generalised hyperarousal. In addition she describes lifelong difficulty regulating emotions with frequent explosive anger and sustained periods of shutdown, a deeply negative self-view (she describes herself as fundamentally broken and shameful), and pervasive difficulty maintaining any close relationship, including with her current partner and her two adult children.

She has not previously been diagnosed with a mental illness. She has no history of psychosis or mania. She uses alcohol occasionally but not to problematic levels, and she takes no regular medication.

data_table.Examination: MSE reveals PTSD phenomena as above with additional pervasive affect dysregulation and interpersonal impairment.

lead_in: Which is the single most accurate ICD-11 diagnosis?

options.text: Post-traumatic stress disorder in the absence of any personality-level disturbance
options.rationale: PTSD captures her re-experiencing, avoidance and hyperarousal but does not code the additional pervasive disturbances in self-organisation that dominate her presentation (Source: ICD-11).

options.text: Borderline personality disorder without concurrent trauma-related disorder recognised
options.rationale: BPD and complex PTSD overlap significantly, but the diagnostic anchor here is a clearly identifiable pattern of chronic developmental trauma with core PTSD symptoms plus disturbances in self-organisation. Distinguishing features favouring complex PTSD include stable negative self-view (not oscillating), less fear of abandonment, and identifiable trauma origin (Source: ICD-11).

options.text: Dissociative identity disorder with trauma-related re-experiencing as the leading presentation
options.rationale: DID requires two or more distinct personality states with recurrent gaps in autobiographical memory; not described in this vignette (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Complex post-traumatic stress disorder with disturbances in self-organisation
options.rationale: ICD-11 complex PTSD requires the three core PTSD clusters (re-experiencing, avoidance, threat sense) plus the disturbances in self-organisation triad: affect dysregulation, negative self-concept and interpersonal difficulties. She meets all three additional criteria on a background of chronic, developmentally-timed interpersonal trauma. This coding matters because complex PTSD often requires longer, phase-based therapy prior to trauma-focused work (Source: ICD-11; Phoenix Australia Australian Guidelines for PTSD).
source_refs: Phoenix Australia Australian Guidelines for PTSD

options.text: Persistent depressive disorder as the primary trauma-related diagnostic category
options.rationale: PDD requires depressed mood most days for 2 or more years; this description does not centre on chronic depressed mood as the primary phenomenon (Source: DSM-5-TR).

explanation.summary: ICD-11 complex PTSD adds the disturbances in self-organisation triad (affect dysregulation, negative self-concept, interpersonal difficulties) to the standard PTSD clusters, typically following prolonged or repeated developmentally-timed interpersonal trauma. Recognition changes therapy sequencing.
key_points: ICD-11 complex PTSD adds affect dysregulation + negative self-concept + interpersonal difficulty
Overlaps with BPD but is distinguished by identifiable chronic trauma origin
Phase-based therapy: stabilisation, then trauma processing, then reintegration
DSM-5-TR does not have a complex PTSD code; use PTSD with dissociative subtype or specifiers
explanation.pearls: In context, complex PTSD is a helpful frame for adult survivors of chronic childhood abuse and often reframes clinicians away from BPD-first diagnoses that carry stigma.

sources.label: Phoenix Australia Australian Guidelines for PTSD

subtopic_detail: Illness anxiety disorder - test-negative but preoccupation persists
stem:
A 39-year-old accountant has attended your practice on 14 occasions in the past 12 months, each visit motivated by a new fear of a serious illness. Over the past 8 months he has been convinced at different times he had bowel cancer, motor neuron disease, a brain tumour and thyroid cancer. Each concern has been triggered by minor bodily sensations such as passing normal-textured stool of variable colour, a leg twitch after exercise or a fleeting sensation of neck swelling.

Despite two normal colonoscopies, an MRI brain, thyroid ultrasound and repeated bloods including TFTs and creatine kinase, his fears settle briefly then reappear with the next symptom. He spends 3 to 4 hours daily searching the internet for illness information. He does not describe any prominent physical symptom that dominates his day - his distress centres on the fear of having or acquiring a serious illness.

data_table.Examination: Unremarkable. No focal neurological signs, no palpable thyroid nodule.
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, LFTs, TSH, CK within reference. Colonoscopy x2 normal. MRI brain normal. Thyroid ultrasound normal.

lead_in: Which is the single most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Delusional disorder, somatic subtype, persistent presentation
options.rationale: Delusional disorder requires a fixed false belief held with delusional intensity that is not amenable to negative testing; this patient's beliefs settle briefly after negative investigations, indicating they are not held with delusional certainty (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Somatic symptom disorder, persistent care-seeking type
options.rationale: SSD requires one or more distressing somatic symptoms that disrupt daily life with excessive thoughts, feelings or behaviours related to those symptoms; the anchoring feature is the SYMPTOM. This patient does not have a persistent dominant physical symptom - his distress centres on illness fear, not on a symptom (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Obsessive-compulsive disorder, contamination and checking subtype
options.rationale: OCD would require ego-dystonic obsessions with structured compensatory compulsions; his illness fears are more ego-syntonic (he believes the concern is warranted) and his searching is reassurance seeking rather than a stereotyped compulsion (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Factitious disorder imposed on self, chronic recurrent type
options.rationale: Factitious disorder requires deceptive falsification of physical or psychological signs or symptoms in the absence of obvious external reward; this patient is not fabricating symptoms (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Illness anxiety disorder, care-seeking predominant type
options.rationale: DSM-5 illness anxiety disorder is defined by preoccupation with having or acquiring a serious illness, absence of or only mild somatic symptoms, high anxiety about health, excessive health-related behaviours (frequent checking, reassurance seeking, online searching) or maladaptive avoidance, and duration of at least 6 months. This vignette fits precisely (Source: DSM-5-TR; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: The core discriminator between illness anxiety disorder and somatic symptom disorder in DSM-5 is whether physical symptoms are prominent (SSD) or minimal (IAD). Both cluster with health-focused distress but the treatment approach centres on care-seeking behaviour patterns.
key_points: IAD: preoccupation with having illness, minimal or absent physical symptoms, 6 months
SSD: distressing physical symptom(s) plus disproportionate thoughts, 6 months
OCD is distinguished by ego-dystonic obsessions with structured compulsions
Management: CBT with response prevention (limit reassurance seeking and testing), regular scheduled GP visits with a single provider, treat comorbid depression or anxiety
explanation.pearls: In context, structured brief regular visits with the same GP break the reassurance-seeking cycle better than open-access reactive visits.

subtopic_detail: Body dysmorphic disorder - muscle dysmorphia subtype
stem:
A 22-year-old male gym instructor presents at the urging of his mother. He weighs 96 kg at 178 cm tall (BMI 30 kg/m2, with visibly increased muscle mass and low body fat). He spends 4 hours daily at the gym, mirrors constantly to check his shoulders and chest, weighs and photographs his physique twice daily, and describes himself as too small and skinny. He has withdrawn from a serious relationship and left an accounting cadetship to work in a gym where he feels less exposed.

He volunteers that he has been injecting testosterone enanthate 500 mg intramuscularly weekly for the last 6 months, sourced online, and takes clenbuterol during cuts. He has no other psychiatric history and denies eating disorder pathology in the classic sense - his intake is high in protein, not restricted overall. He has no insight into how others perceive his appearance and is highly distressed when unable to train.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88, BP 148/94, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 98%, temperature 36.6.
data_table.Examination: Heavily muscled, acne over back and shoulders, mild gynaecomastia, testicular atrophy on examination.
data_table.Investigations: Haematocrit 0.54 (RR 0.40-0.50), LFTs mildly deranged, LH and FSH suppressed.

lead_in: Which is the single most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Anabolic androgenic steroid use disorder as the primary and sole diagnosis
options.rationale: AAS use disorder is present and clinically important, but the primary driver of the presentation is BDD (muscle dysmorphia) that leads to the AAS use; both diagnoses can co-exist, with BDD being primary here (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Anorexia nervosa, atypical subtype without a low body weight criterion
options.rationale: Anorexia nervosa requires restriction of energy intake with a fear of gaining weight; this patient eats large volumes and aims to gain muscle mass, which does not fit AN pathology (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Body dysmorphic disorder, muscle dysmorphia subtype presentation
options.rationale: DSM-5 body dysmorphic disorder requires preoccupation with a perceived defect not observable to others (here, being too small despite obvious high muscle mass), repetitive behaviours (mirror checking, grooming, photographing, comparing) and functional impairment. Muscle dysmorphia is a specifier for BDD with preoccupation with insufficient muscularity, common in young men, and often associated with AAS use (Source: DSM-5-TR; RANZCP CPG: OCD and Related Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP CPG: OCD and Related Disorders

options.text: Obsessive-compulsive disorder, ordering and symmetry subtype
options.rationale: OCD requires obsessions and compulsions; his mirror checking and grooming resemble compulsions but the driving belief centres on appearance rather than contamination or magical thinking, placing him in BDD (which is in the OCD spectrum but distinct) (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Narcissistic personality disorder with grandiose subtype presentation
options.rationale: NPD requires a pervasive pattern of grandiosity, need for admiration and lack of empathy; his presentation centres on distress about perceived inadequacy and avoidance rather than grandiosity (Source: DSM-5-TR).

explanation.summary: Muscle dysmorphia is a DSM-5 body dysmorphic disorder specifier defined by preoccupation with insufficient muscularity, common in young men and strongly associated with anabolic androgenic steroid use, gynaecomastia, HPG axis suppression and cardiovascular harm.
key_points: BDD sits in the OCD-related disorders chapter of DSM-5
Muscle dysmorphia subtype: preoccupation with insufficient muscularity
AAS use frequently co-occurs and produces gynaecomastia, testicular atrophy, polycythaemia and hepatotoxicity
First-line management: SSRI at OCD-range doses plus CBT with mirror-retraining and response prevention; harm reduction for AAS
explanation.pearls: In context, screen for AAS use in any muscular young man presenting with mood, aggression, gynaecomastia or polycythaemia. The BDD driver often outlasts the AAS behaviour.

sources.label: RANZCP CPG: OCD and Related Disorders

subtopic_detail: Selective mutism - discrimination from autism spectrum
stem:
You are a GP registrar seeing a 6-year-old girl brought by her mother because she has never spoken at school since starting reception two years ago. Her teacher reports that she plays alongside other children, follows instructions and completes tasks, but never speaks and communicates by pointing and nodding. Her mother reports that at home she is chatty, tells long stories, argues with her older brother, sings, and has age-appropriate vocabulary and grammar. She also speaks freely at her grandparents' house and to her one close friend on play-dates at home.

She has no history of developmental delay. She reached all milestones on time, makes eye contact with familiar people, engages in imaginative play, shares interests and has no restricted or repetitive behaviours. She is otherwise healthy.

data_table.Examination: Cooperative with mother, watchful with you, does not speak. Age-appropriate play. Normal hearing screen documented.

lead_in: Which is the single most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Selective mutism, situationally-restricted subtype
options.rationale: DSM-5 selective mutism describes consistent failure to speak in specific social situations where speech is expected (school) despite speaking normally in other situations (home, grandparents), lasting more than 1 month (beyond the first month of school), interfering with function, and not better explained by a communication disorder or ASD. This vignette meets criteria (Source: DSM-5-TR; RCH Melbourne CPG).

options.text: Autism spectrum disorder, level 1 subtype
options.rationale: ASD requires persistent deficits in social communication AND restricted repetitive behaviours across contexts; her communication is age-appropriate at home and she engages in typical imaginative play with normal social reciprocity in comfortable settings (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Reactive attachment disorder, inhibited subtype
options.rationale: RAD requires a history of extremes of insufficient care and consistent inhibited emotionally withdrawn behaviour toward adult caregivers; this vignette describes normal attachment behaviour at home (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Expressive language disorder, developmental type
options.rationale: Expressive language disorder produces reduced expressive vocabulary or grammar across all contexts; this child speaks fluently at home with age-appropriate language (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Social anxiety disorder alone as a standalone diagnosis
options.rationale: Social anxiety disorder in children can co-occur with selective mutism (up to 90% overlap) but the specific feature of being able to speak fluently in some contexts and completely mute in others meets the more specific selective mutism diagnosis (Source: DSM-5-TR).

explanation.summary: Selective mutism is an anxiety disorder characterised by failure to speak in specific social situations despite typical speech in others. It is distinguished from ASD by preserved communication and reciprocity in comfortable settings, and from expressive language disorder by normal language at home.
key_points: Selective mutism: mute in specific settings, fluent elsewhere, over 1 month, interferes with function
Distinguishing from ASD: normal social reciprocity and communication in comfortable contexts
Distinguishing from language disorder: age-appropriate language when speaking
First-line management: behavioural therapy with graded exposure and stimulus fading; SSRI (fluoxetine) if severe or refractory
explanation.pearls: In context, the school environment is the therapy setting. Coordinate with the school psychologist and teacher for structured stimulus-fading rather than pressuring the child to speak.

subtopic_detail: Adult separation anxiety disorder - DSM-5 recognition in adulthood
stem:
A 34-year-old woman presents to her GP with 3 years of increasing distress around any separation from her partner. She experiences intense worry that harm will come to him whenever they are apart, checks on him by text every 15 minutes when he is away, and has twice left work early because of fear that he had been in a car accident when he did not answer immediately. She has nightmares of losing him. Physical complaints of nausea and stomach ache occur when he goes on interstate work trips.

She has no history of a childhood anxiety disorder and functioned well through university and her twenties in previous relationships. Her partner is well, works in an office role and has never had a serious accident or illness. She has no personal history of trauma, no substance use and no other current psychiatric symptoms.

data_table.Examination: Anxious; no low mood, no psychotic features.

lead_in: Which is the single most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Panic disorder with agoraphobia specifier as the primary diagnosis
options.rationale: Panic disorder requires recurrent unexpected discrete panic attacks; the vignette describes ongoing anxiety tied to a specific trigger rather than paroxysmal peak-fear episodes (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Dependent personality disorder in adult onset form
options.rationale: DPD is a lifelong pervasive pattern of submissive and clinging behaviour with a broad need to be taken care of, not tied to a single attachment figure; this presentation is separation-specific and started in adulthood (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Obsessive-compulsive disorder, checking and reassurance subtype
options.rationale: OCD would require ego-dystonic obsessions with compulsive rituals; her checking is anxiety-driven reassurance seeking rather than a stereotyped compulsion, and the concerns are not experienced as intrusive and unwanted in the OCD sense (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Generalised anxiety disorder, single-domain presentation
options.rationale: GAD requires excessive worry across multiple domains on more days than not for 6 months; her worry centres specifically on separation from an attachment figure and is not multi-domain (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Separation anxiety disorder, adult-onset attachment-figure form
options.rationale: DSM-5 removed the childhood-only requirement in 2013. Adult separation anxiety disorder is diagnosed when there is developmentally inappropriate excessive fear of separation from major attachment figures, persistent worry about losing them or harm coming to them, reluctance to be apart, nightmares of separation, and physical symptoms on separation, with duration of 6 months or more in adults (Source: DSM-5-TR; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: DSM-5 formally recognises separation anxiety disorder in adults, requiring 6 months of developmentally inappropriate excessive fear of separation from a major attachment figure with functional impairment.
key_points: Adult separation anxiety disorder is a valid DSM-5 diagnosis since 2013
6-month duration in adults, 4 weeks in children
First-line management is CBT with graded separation exposure
SSRI is second-line and can be considered when impairment persists
explanation.pearls: In context, separation anxiety in adults is under-recognised and frequently misdiagnosed as GAD, dependent personality disorder or relationship difficulty. Ask specifically about the trigger pattern.

subtopic_detail: Panic disorder with agoraphobia - interoceptive exposure rationale
stem:
A 37-year-old woman with 4 years of panic disorder attends for CBT with a clinical psychologist. She has now developed marked agoraphobia and only leaves the house when accompanied. She has taken 6 weeks off her administrative role. She has been on sertraline 100 mg orally daily for 8 weeks with partial reduction in panic frequency. Her psychologist plans to begin exposure work.

She has learned to identify her early panic symptoms (palpitations, breathlessness, depersonalisation) and reports that these bodily sensations are what she most fears. She has been managing panic by immediately sitting down, sipping cold water, and using slow breathing to abort the sensations before they build. She has no cardiac history and a recent 12-lead ECG was normal.

data_table.Examination: Anxious but composed in the clinic room.
data_table.Investigations: TSH, FBC, UEC within reference. ECG normal.

lead_in: Which exposure component is the most important target for her CBT?

options.text: Interoceptive exposure to feared bodily sensations with concurrent response prevention of safety behaviours during the exercise
options.rationale: In panic disorder the core fear is of internal bodily sensations (catastrophic misinterpretation), and safety behaviours such as sitting down, sipping water and controlled breathing prevent disconfirmation of catastrophic beliefs and maintain the disorder. Interoceptive exposure deliberately reproduces the feared sensations (hyperventilation, spinning, straw-breathing) without safety behaviours to enable extinction learning (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Anxiety disorders; RANZCP CPG: Anxiety Disorders).

options.text: Cognitive restructuring of catastrophic thoughts without any accompanying behavioural exposure component in the treatment plan
options.rationale: Cognitive restructuring alone is less effective than combined cognitive-behavioural intervention with exposure in panic disorder; behavioural extinction of the fear response requires actual exposure (Source: RANZCP CPG: Anxiety Disorders).

options.text: Situational exposure with continued slow-breathing safety behaviour to abort panic during each exposure attempt
options.rationale: Continuing safety behaviours (slow breathing to abort sensations) during exposure prevents disconfirmation of catastrophic beliefs about bodily sensations and blocks extinction learning; safety behaviours must be dropped during exposure (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Anxiety disorders).

options.text: Progressive muscle relaxation training as the primary standalone intervention with agoraphobia work deferred to later sessions
options.rationale: Relaxation alone functions similarly to a safety behaviour in panic disorder and is not first-line; it can be a component but not the primary intervention (Source: RANZCP CPG: Anxiety Disorders).

options.text: Eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing (EMDR) as the primary intervention for her established panic and agoraphobia
options.rationale: EMDR is a trauma-focused therapy for PTSD; it is not first-line for panic disorder in the absence of trauma (Source: Phoenix Australia Australian Guidelines for PTSD).
source_refs: Phoenix Australia Australian Guidelines for PTSD

explanation.summary: Panic disorder is driven by catastrophic misinterpretation of bodily sensations. Interoceptive exposure - deliberately reproducing the feared sensations without safety behaviours - is the highest-yield CBT component. Situational exposure adds agoraphobia recovery.
key_points: Interoceptive exposure: hyperventilation, spinning, straw-breathing, physical exertion
Drop safety behaviours (breathing exercises, sipping water, sitting down) during exposure
Add in-vivo situational exposure to feared places (shops, transport) to address agoraphobia
CBT plus SSRI outperforms either modality alone at 6 to 12 months
explanation.pearls: In context, safety behaviours look protective but function as the maintaining mechanism. Naming and dropping them is often the pivotal therapeutic move.

sources.label: Phoenix Australia Australian Guidelines for PTSD

subtopic_detail: Postpartum OCD - intrusive harm thoughts distinct from postpartum psychosis
stem:
You are called by the child and family health nurse about a 31-year-old woman she has just visited at home. The patient is 6 weeks postpartum after an uncomplicated first pregnancy. Over the last 3 weeks she has developed distressing intrusive images of harming her baby - specifically, of dropping her over the balcony rail or in the bath. She describes the thoughts as horrifying, alien and unwanted, and she is deeply ashamed. She has responded by refusing to bathe her baby alone, avoiding the balcony entirely, and asking her partner to check on the baby repeatedly during the night.

She denies wanting to harm her baby, has no plan or intent, and is not hearing voices telling her to act. She has no confusion, elated mood, grandiose beliefs or paranoid ideas. She has no personal or family history of bipolar disorder or postpartum psychosis. She is breastfeeding exclusively and there is no history of substance use. EPDS is 18. Her interaction with the baby during the visit was warm and appropriate.

data_table.Examination: Tearful, anxious, insight preserved, no thought disorder, no psychotic features. MSE reveals ego-dystonic intrusive imagery.
data_table.Investigations: TSH within reference at 4 weeks postpartum. FBC within reference.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Report to child protection as a mandatory notification of imminent risk of harm from a mother describing thoughts of dropping her baby
options.rationale: Ego-dystonic intrusive thoughts in OCD are not associated with acting on them and do not meet the threshold for a child protection notification of imminent risk. Notification without an actual risk finding damages the therapeutic relationship and delays appropriate treatment. Document risk assessment thoroughly (Source: RANZCP CPG: Perinatal Mental Health; COPE Perinatal Mental Health Guidelines).

options.text: Offer CBT with response prevention plus sertraline commenced at 25 mg titrated to 100 mg with breastfeeding maintained
options.rationale: This is postpartum-onset OCD with ego-dystonic intrusive harm thoughts and behavioural response (avoidance and reassurance seeking). Intrusive thoughts of harm to the baby occur in up to 50% of new mothers to some extent; the OCD threshold is met by distress, functional impact and structured avoidance or checking. Management is CBT with ERP plus SSRI. Sertraline is the preferred SSRI in breastfeeding due to lowest infant serum concentrations (Source: COPE Perinatal Mental Health Guidelines; RANZCP CPG: Perinatal Mental Health; Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Commence olanzapine 5 mg orally at night as first-line pharmacotherapy for postpartum intrusive thoughts of harming the baby
options.rationale: Olanzapine is used in postpartum psychosis or severe mood-with-psychotic-features; this presentation is OCD, not psychosis. First-line pharmacotherapy is an SSRI (Source: RANZCP CPG: Perinatal Mental Health; Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Arrange urgent involuntary admission to a mother-baby unit for suspected postpartum psychosis with mandatory temporary separation from the baby
options.rationale: The clinical picture is not consistent with postpartum psychosis: no confusion, no elated or paranoid mood, no delusions, no hallucinations, preserved insight, and ego-dystonic intrusive thoughts (she is horrified by them, not endorsing them). Involuntary admission and separating the baby would compound harm without addressing the actual disorder (Source: RANZCP CPG: Perinatal Mental Health; COPE Perinatal Mental Health Guidelines).

options.text: Recommend she cease breastfeeding immediately today before any SSRI is prescribed or CBT referral is initiated
options.rationale: Breastfeeding does not need to stop when starting sertraline; sertraline has minimal infant serum concentrations and is compatible with breastfeeding, and stopping breastfeeding compounds distress without benefit (Source: COPE Perinatal Mental Health Guidelines; Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: Postpartum-onset OCD frequently presents with ego-dystonic intrusive thoughts of harming the baby. It is distinguished from postpartum psychosis by preserved insight, absence of psychotic features, and the thoughts being unwanted and distressing rather than endorsed. Management is CBT with ERP plus sertraline, with breastfeeding maintained.
key_points: Postpartum OCD: ego-dystonic intrusive harm thoughts + avoidance or checking, insight preserved
Postpartum psychosis: confusion, elated or paranoid mood, delusions, hallucinations, loss of insight, medical emergency
Sertraline is the preferred SSRI in breastfeeding (lowest infant serum concentrations)
CBT with response prevention targets avoidance and reassurance seeking
Child protection notification is not indicated when the thoughts are ego-dystonic and there is no plan, intent or objective risk
explanation.pearls: In context, distinguishing postpartum OCD from postpartum psychosis is the single most consequential judgment in perinatal psychiatry. Getting it wrong in either direction causes major harm.

subtopic_detail: Acute stress reaction ICD-11 vs acute stress disorder DSM-5
stem:
You are the resident on the trauma ward reviewing a 27-year-old cyclist 3 days after a high-speed collision with a car. He sustained a fractured tibia now internally fixed and multiple minor abrasions. He is otherwise medically stable. Over the last 72 hours he has been tearful, has vivid intrusive memories of the impact, has slept poorly with nightmares, feels emotionally detached from his family visiting, and startles at loud noises on the ward. He is very distressed but is oriented, cooperative with rehabilitation, engaging with his physiotherapist and is able to describe the events coherently.

He has no personal or family history of psychiatric illness, no substance use disorder, no prior trauma exposure and no premorbid anxiety condition. The trauma social worker asks whether this warrants a formal psychiatric diagnosis and referral to a trauma-focused therapy service, and whether he should be prescribed anything today.

data_table.Examination: Distressed but engaged; MSE consistent with acute stress phenomena.
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, LFTs within reference. TSH not indicated.

lead_in: Which is the most accurate description of his condition and the most appropriate immediate response?

options.text: Diagnose acute stress disorder now under DSM-5 and start sertraline 50 mg orally daily today to prevent progression to PTSD
options.rationale: DSM-5 acute stress disorder requires nine or more symptoms across five clusters lasting 3 days to 1 month, but early trauma-focused CBT is offered when significant symptoms persist beyond 2 weeks (per Phoenix Australia), not at 72 hours. Routine early pharmacological prophylaxis (including SSRI) does not prevent PTSD and is not recommended in the acute period (Source: Phoenix Australia Australian Guidelines for PTSD; DSM-5-TR).
source_refs: Phoenix Australia Australian Guidelines for PTSD

options.text: Provide single-session critical incident stress debriefing today at the bedside to prevent the development of subsequent PTSD
options.rationale: Single-session critical incident stress debriefing is not recommended and Cochrane and Phoenix Australia evidence indicates it may worsen outcomes for some individuals; it is specifically advised against (Source: Phoenix Australia Australian Guidelines for PTSD).
source_refs: Phoenix Australia Australian Guidelines for PTSD

options.text: Provide psychological first aid with watchful waiting and review at 2 to 4 weeks, referring only if symptoms persist or worsen
options.rationale: ICD-11 explicitly classifies acute stress reaction as a normal transient response to exceptional trauma (outside the mental disorders chapter), typically resolving within days to a week. Immediate management is psychological first aid, practical support, and watchful waiting. Phoenix Australia recommends against routine debriefing and against early pharmacological intervention, with formal trauma-focused therapy indicated only if significant symptoms persist beyond 2 to 4 weeks (Source: ICD-11 QE84 Acute stress reaction; Phoenix Australia Australian Guidelines for PTSD).
source_refs: Phoenix Australia Australian Guidelines for PTSD

options.text: Commence diazepam 5 mg orally three times daily for the first two weeks post-injury to prevent the development of PTSD
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines are recommended against in the acute post-trauma period; they impair extinction learning and are associated with a HIGHER incidence of subsequent PTSD in cohort data (Source: Phoenix Australia Australian Guidelines for PTSD).
source_refs: Phoenix Australia Australian Guidelines for PTSD

options.text: Diagnose PTSD now on the strength of his intrusive memories and start prazosin overnight to treat the nightmares he is experiencing
options.rationale: PTSD requires the symptom cluster to persist for more than 1 month by DSM-5 criteria; a diagnosis cannot be made at 72 hours and prazosin is used for treatment-resistant nightmares in established PTSD (Source: DSM-5-TR; Phoenix Australia Australian Guidelines for PTSD).
source_refs: Phoenix Australia Australian Guidelines for PTSD

explanation.summary: ICD-11 acute stress reaction is a normal transient response to major trauma, coded outside the mental disorders chapter. DSM-5 acute stress disorder is a mental disorder diagnosed between 3 days and 1 month post-trauma. Both classification systems point to the same acute-phase management: psychological first aid, watchful waiting, avoid early debriefing, avoid benzodiazepines, and refer for trauma-focused CBT only if symptoms persist.
key_points: ICD-11 acute stress reaction: normal transient reaction, not a mental disorder
DSM-5 acute stress disorder: 3 days to 1 month, nine symptoms across five clusters
PTSD requires symptoms for over 1 month
Cochrane evidence: single-session debriefing not recommended and may harm
Early benzodiazepines associated with higher subsequent PTSD incidence
Refer for trauma-focused CBT if significant symptoms persist beyond 2 to 4 weeks
explanation.pearls: In context, the temptation to medicalise a normal acute reaction is strong. Watchful waiting with practical support and clear follow-up is evidence-based and often sufficient.

sources.label: Phoenix Australia Australian Guidelines for PTSD
